anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: What is the classic deficit of a middle cerebral artery (MCA) stroke?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: Contralateral weakness & sensory loss of the face & arm > leg, plus aphasia (dominant hemisphere) or hemineglect (non-dominant); eyes may deviate towards the lesion.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: What is the classic deficit of an anterior cerebral artery (ACA) stroke?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: Contralateral weakness & sensory loss of the leg > arm (the leg is on the medial homunculus), often with abulia/personality change.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: What visual defect follows a posterior cerebral artery (PCA) stroke?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: A contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing (occipital cortex; the macula has dual MCA/PCA supply).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: What characterises a lacunar stroke, and where?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: A small deep-perforator infarct (internal capsule, thalamus, pons) giving pure motor, pure sensory or ataxic-hemiparesis syndromes with NO cortical signs (no aphasia/neglect).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: Why does an MCA stroke spare the leg while an ACA stroke affects it?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: The leg area of the homunculus lies on the medial surface (ACA territory); the face & hand lie on the lateral surface (MCA territory).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: What is the 'rule of crossed signs' in brainstem lesions?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: A brainstem lesion causes an ipsilateral cranial-nerve deficit with contralateral long-tract (limb) signs — the crossed pattern localises the lesion to the brainstem.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: Describe Weber's syndrome.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: A midbrain stroke (PCA branches) → ipsilateral CN III palsy (down-and-out, dilated pupil, ptosis) + contralateral hemiparesis.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: Describe the lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: A PICA/vertebral infarct: ipsilateral Horner’s, facial pain/temperature loss (CN V), ataxia, dysphagia/hoarseness (CN IX/X), vertigo/nystagmus; contralateral body pain/temperature loss — with no limb weakness.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: Describe medial medullary syndrome.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: Ipsilateral tongue weakness (CN XII) with contralateral hemiparesis and loss of proprioception/vibration (anterior spinal/vertebral artery).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: What is locked-in syndrome and where is the lesion?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: A ventral pontine (basilar) lesion → quadriplegia and anarthria with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements/blinking.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: Contrast Broca's and Wernicke's aphasia.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: Broca’s (inferior frontal) — non-fluent, effortful speech, comprehension intact. Wernicke’s (superior temporal) — fluent but meaningless speech, comprehension impaired.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: What deficit follows a lesion of the arcuate fasciculus?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: Conduction aphasia — fluent speech and preserved comprehension but impaired repetition (it connects Wernicke’s to Broca’s area).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: What is Gerstmann's syndrome and where does it localise?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: A dominant parietal (angular gyrus) lesion → acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia and left–right disorientation.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: What sign follows a non-dominant parietal lobe lesion?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: Contralateral hemispatial neglect (and constructional/dressing apraxia).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: How do you distinguish an upper (UMN) from a lower (LMN) motor neuron facial palsy?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: A UMN lesion (e.g. stroke) spares the forehead (bilateral cortical input to the upper face); a LMN lesion (e.g. Bell’s palsy) paralyses the whole half of the face.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: Describe the deficits of Brown-Séquard (cord hemisection).
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: Ipsilateral motor weakness & dorsal-column loss (proprioception/vibration) below the lesion; contralateral pain & temperature loss starting 1–2 segments below.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: What is spared in anterior cord syndrome, and why?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: The dorsal columns (proprioception & vibration) are spared because they are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries; the anterior spinal artery territory (motor + spinothalamic) is lost.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: What is the pattern of central cord syndrome?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: A “cape” (suspended) loss of pain & temperature across the shoulders, with weakness that is worse in the upper than lower limbs (e.g. syrinx or hyperextension injury).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: What tracts are affected in subacute combined degeneration, and its cause?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: Vitamin B₁₂ deficiency damages the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts (± spinocerebellar) → sensory ataxia, loss of vibration/proprioception and UMN weakness.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: Distinguish conus medullaris from cauda equina syndrome.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: Conus — early, symmetric saddle anaesthesia & bladder/bowel dysfunction, mixed UMN/LMN. Cauda equina — asymmetric LMN flaccid weakness, radicular pain, later urinary retention; a surgical emergency.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: What happens in uncal (transtentorial) herniation?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: The uncus compresses CN III → a fixed, dilated (‘blown’) pupil and down-and-out eye, then contralateral hemiparesis (or ipsilateral via Kernohan’s notch) and coma.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: Why must you never do a lumbar puncture in a patient with a mass and raised ICP?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: Removing CSF can precipitate tonsillar herniation (cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum) → fatal brainstem compression.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: What is Cushing's triad, and what does it indicate?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration (e.g. Cheyne–Stokes) — a late sign of dangerously raised intracranial pressure.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: An extradural (epidural) haematoma: vessel, history and CT appearance?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: The middle meningeal artery (temporal bone fracture at the pterion); a lucid interval then rapid deterioration; a biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdensity that does not cross sutures.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: A subdural haematoma: vessel, typical patient and CT appearance?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: Torn bridging veins; elderly, alcoholic or anticoagulated patients with fluctuating consciousness; a crescent-shaped collection that crosses sutures.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: What causes a spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage and how does it present?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: Rupture of a berry (saccular) aneurysm of the circle of Willis → thunderclap (‘worst-ever’) headache and meningism; associated with polycystic kidney disease and Ehlers–Danlos.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: Name the cerebellar signs (DANISH) and their laterality.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: Dysdiadochokinesia, Ataxia, Nystagmus, Intention tremor, Scanning speech, Hypotonia — the signs are ipsilateral to the lesion.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: What is hemiballismus and where is the lesion?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: Violent, large-amplitude flinging movements of the contralateral limbs, from a lesion of the subthalamic nucleus (often a lacunar stroke).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.front: What are the features of Horner's syndrome and some causes?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.back: Miosis, partial ptosis and anhidrosis (± enophthalmos) from a sympathetic-pathway lesion — e.g. Pancoast tumour, lateral medullary syndrome, carotid dissection.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: Which sulcus separates the frontal from the parietal lobe, and what lies on each side?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: The central sulcus (of Rolando): the precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex) lies in front and the postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex) behind.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: What does the lateral fissure (of Sylvius) separate?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: It separates the temporal lobe (below) from the frontal and parietal lobes (above); the insula lies deep within it.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: Which sulcus contains the primary visual cortex?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: The calcarine sulcus of the occipital lobe (Brodmann area 17).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: How many layers does the neocortex have, versus the allocortex?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: The neocortex (~90%) has six layers (I molecular → VI multiform); the allocortex (hippocampus, olfactory cortex) has three.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: What is special about cortical layer IV?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: The internal granular layer receives thalamic sensory input; it is thick in sensory (‘granular’) cortex and absent in motor (‘agranular’) cortex.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: Where are the Betz cells, and what do they do?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: Giant pyramidal neurons in layer V of the primary motor cortex; they contribute the large axons of the corticospinal tract.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: Which cortical layers give rise to cortico-cortical (association/commissural) fibres, and which projects back to the thalamus?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: Layers II and III give cortico-cortical fibres; layer VI projects back to the thalamus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: Where is the primary motor cortex and its Brodmann number?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: The precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe — Brodmann area 4; it controls contralateral voluntary movement via the corticospinal tract.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: Where is the primary somatosensory cortex and its Brodmann numbers?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: The postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe — Brodmann areas 3, 1 & 2.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: What is Brodmann area 6, and what does it do?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: The premotor and supplementary motor cortex (anterior to area 4) — it plans and sequences movements.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: What does the frontal eye field (area 8) do?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: It drives voluntary conjugate gaze to the opposite side; a destructive lesion causes the eyes to deviate towards the lesion.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: Where is the primary visual cortex and its Brodmann number?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: Around the calcarine sulcus of the occipital lobe — Brodmann area 17 (striate cortex); areas 18 & 19 are visual association cortex.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: Where is the primary auditory cortex and its Brodmann numbers?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: In Heschl’s gyri of the superior temporal gyrus — Brodmann areas 41 & 42 (tonotopically organised).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: Where is Broca's area and what are its Brodmann numbers?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: The inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere — Brodmann areas 44 & 45; it controls motor/expressive speech.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: Where is Wernicke's area and its Brodmann number?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: The posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere — Brodmann area 22; it governs language comprehension.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: Describe the language loop from comprehension to speech.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: Wernicke’s area (22) comprehends language → the arcuate fasciculus conveys it → Broca’s area (44/45) produces speech; the angular (39) & supramarginal (40) gyri handle reading/writing.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: What is the somatotopic map of the motor/sensory cortex called, and how is the body arranged?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: The homunculus: the leg & foot are on the medial surface (paracentral lobule, ACA territory) and the face, hand & tongue on the lateral surface (MCA territory).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: Why are the hand and face so large on the homunculus?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: Cortical representation is proportional to dexterity/sensitivity, not size — so the hand, lips and face occupy disproportionately large areas and the trunk very little.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: How does the homunculus explain ACA versus MCA stroke patterns?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: The ACA supplies the medial (leg) homunculus → leg > arm weakness; the MCA supplies the lateral (face/arm) homunculus → face/arm > leg weakness.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: Define the three types of cerebral white-matter fibres.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: Association — connect areas within one hemisphere; commissural — connect the two hemispheres; projection — connect the cortex to subcortical structures/cord.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: Give examples of association fibres.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: The superior longitudinal/arcuate fasciculus, uncinate fasciculus, cingulum and inferior longitudinal fasciculus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: What is the largest commissural tract, and what does its section cause?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: The corpus callosum; its section (‘split brain’) produces disconnection syndromes (e.g. left-hand agraphia/tactile anomia).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: Name the parts of the internal capsule and what the posterior limb carries.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: Anterior limb, genu and posterior limb. The posterior limb carries the corticospinal tract (and sensory fibres); a lacunar stroke here causes a pure motor hemiparesis.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: What fibres run in the genu of the internal capsule?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: Corticobulbar fibres — to the motor nuclei of the cranial nerves.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: Which hemisphere is dominant in most people, and for what functions?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: The left hemisphere in ~95% (including most left-handers) — for language, calculation and analytical/sequential processing.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: What functions are lateralised to the non-dominant (usually right) hemisphere?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: Spatial awareness, prosody, face recognition and music; non-dominant parietal lesions cause contralateral hemineglect.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.front: What is the primary gustatory (taste) cortex region?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.back: The insula and frontal operculum (with the adjacent parietal area, Brodmann area 43).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: Which nuclei make up the striatum, and what is its role?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: The caudate nucleus + putamen = the striatum, the input zone of the basal ganglia (receives cortical afferents).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: What is the lentiform (lenticular) nucleus?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: The putamen + globus pallidus (external GPe and internal GPi segments).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: What are the output nuclei of the basal ganglia, and what do they do at rest?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: The globus pallidus internus (GPi) and substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr); they tonically inhibit the thalamus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: Which part of the substantia nigra is dopaminergic?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: The pars compacta (SNc) — it supplies dopamine to the striatum; the pars reticulata (SNr) is an output nucleus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: Trace the direct pathway and its net effect.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: Cortex → striatum (D1) → inhibits GPi/SNr → disinhibits the thalamus → thalamus excites cortex. Net effect: promotes movement (‘GO’).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: Trace the indirect pathway and its net effect.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: Cortex → striatum (D2) → inhibits GPe → disinhibits STN → STN excites GPi/SNr → GPi inhibits the thalamus. Net effect: suppresses movement (‘STOP’).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: How does dopamine from the SNc modulate the two pathways?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: It excites the direct pathway (D1 receptors) and inhibits the indirect pathway (D2 receptors) — both actions promote movement.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: Why does loss of dopamine cause a hypokinetic disorder?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: Without dopamine the direct (go) pathway is under-driven and the indirect (stop) pathway over-active → the thalamus is over-inhibited → reduced movement (Parkinsonism).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: What is the lesion and clinical picture of Parkinson's disease?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: Degeneration of dopaminergic SNc neurons → a hypokinetic syndrome: resting ‘pill-rolling’ tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia and postural instability.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: What is the lesion and clinical picture of Huntington's disease?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: Loss of GABAergic striatal (caudate) neurons of the indirect pathway → a hyperkinetic syndrome: chorea, dementia and behavioural change (autosomal dominant CAG-repeat expansion).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: What causes hemiballismus?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: A lesion (often lacunar) of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus → violent, large-amplitude flinging movements of the limbs.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: What basal ganglia structure and signs characterise Wilson's disease?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: Copper deposition in the putamen (and liver) → tremor, dystonia, Kayser–Fleischer rings and liver disease.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: What is the general rule linking dopamine balance to movement disorders?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: Too little dopamine (or over-active indirect pathway) → hypokinetic (Parkinson’s); loss of the indirect brake → hyperkinetic (chorea, hemiballismus).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: What is the overall function of the thalamus?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: It is the great relay station — it relays all sensory modalities except olfaction to the cortex, plus motor and limbic loops.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: What does the VPL nucleus relay, and to where?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: Body sensation (spinothalamic + dorsal column–medial lemniscus) → the primary somatosensory cortex (areas 3,1,2).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: What does the VPM nucleus relay?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: Facial sensation (trigeminal) → the somatosensory cortex (face area); and taste (via the VPM parvocellular part, VPMpc) → the gustatory cortex (insula/frontal operculum).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: What do the lateral (LGN) and medial (MGN) geniculate nuclei relay?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: LGN → vision (optic tract → primary visual cortex, area 17); MGN → hearing (inferior colliculus → primary auditory cortex, areas 41/42).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: What do the VA/VL thalamic nuclei relay?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: Motor information from the basal ganglia and cerebellum → the motor and premotor cortex.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: What is Déjerine–Roussy (thalamic) syndrome?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: A VPL/VPM thalamic stroke → contralateral hemisensory loss followed by severe burning ‘thalamic’ (central post-stroke) pain.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: Name the three lobes of the cerebellum.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: The anterior, posterior and flocculonodular lobes (the flocculonodular lobe is the oldest/vestibular part).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: Name the three layers of the cerebellar cortex, and its only output cell.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: The molecular, Purkinje and granular layers; the Purkinje cell is the sole output — it is inhibitory (GABAergic).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: Name the deep cerebellar nuclei from lateral to medial.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: Dentate, Emboliform, Globose, Fastigial (‘Don’t Eat Greasy Food’).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: What is the function of the vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe)?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: Balance and coordination of eye movements (it connects with the vestibular system).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: What is the function of the spinocerebellum (vermis + paravermis)?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: Control of posture, gait and trunk/proximal limb movement.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: What is the function of the cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres)?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: Planning and coordination of skilled, voluntary limb movements (motor planning).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: What do the three cerebellar peduncles carry?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: Superior — mainly efferent (dentatorubrothalamic → red nucleus/thalamus); middle — afferent (pontocerebellar from the contralateral cortex); inferior — mainly afferent (spinocerebellar & vestibular/olivary input).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: Why are cerebellar signs ipsilateral to the lesion?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: Because cerebellar output double-crosses (the dentatorubrothalamic decussation and then the corticospinal decussation), so the effect returns to the same side as the lesion.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: What are the cerebellar signs (DANISH)?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: Dysdiadochokinesia, Ataxia, Nystagmus, Intention tremor, Scanning speech, Hypotonia.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.front: How do vermis (midline) and hemisphere cerebellar lesions differ clinically?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.back: A vermis/midline lesion causes truncal & gait ataxia (e.g. alcohol, medulloblastoma); a hemisphere lesion causes ipsilateral limb ataxia, intention tremor and past-pointing.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: Name the three parts of the brainstem and their main functions.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: The midbrain, pons and medulla — they conduct all ascending/descending tracts, house cranial-nerve nuclei III–XII, and contain the reticular formation (consciousness & cardiorespiratory control).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: Which cranial nerves arise from each level of the brainstem?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: Midbrain — CN III & IV; pons — CN V, VI, VII & VIII; medulla — CN IX, X, XII (and the cranial/spinal roots of XI). CN I & II are not brainstem nerves.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: How are the cranial-nerve nuclei arranged relative to the sulcus limitans?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: Motor nuclei lie medial and sensory nuclei lie lateral to the sulcus limitans (reflecting the embryonic basal vs alar plates).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: Which cranial-nerve motor nuclei lie closest to the midline (the 'rule of 4')?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: The somatic (GSE) nuclei of the nerves that divide evenly into 12 — III, IV, VI and XII — lie close to the midline; the branchial and visceral motor nuclei lie more laterally.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: Name the three sensory nuclei of the trigeminal nerve and their locations/functions.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: Mesencephalic nucleus (midbrain — proprioception), main/pontine sensory nucleus (pons — fine touch), and spinal nucleus (pons to upper cord — pain & temperature).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: What are the components of the tectum (roof) of the midbrain?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: The corpora quadrigemina: the superior colliculi (visual reflexes) and inferior colliculi (auditory relay).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: What do the cerebral peduncles (crura cerebri) carry, and what lies just behind them?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: The corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts; the substantia nigra lies immediately posterior to them.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: Which structures lie in the midbrain tegmentum around the cerebral aqueduct?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: The red nucleus and the periaqueductal grey (with the oculomotor and trochlear nuclei and the mesencephalic nucleus of V).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: How do CN III and CN IV differ in the way they exit the midbrain?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: CN III emerges anteriorly from the interpeduncular fossa; CN IV is the only cranial nerve to exit dorsally and it decussates before doing so.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: What is Weber's syndrome?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: A lesion of the midbrain cerebral peduncle → ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral hemiparesis (a crossed brainstem sign).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: What does the basilar (ventral) pons contain, and what pathway does it serve?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: The pontine nuclei (relaying cerebral cortex → contralateral cerebellum via the middle cerebellar peduncle) plus the descending corticospinal fibres.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: Where do CN V, VI, VII and VIII exit the pons?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: CN V exits the mid-pons; CN VI, VII and VIII exit at the pontomedullary junction (VII & VIII at the cerebellopontine angle).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: What forms the facial colliculus on the floor of the fourth ventricle?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: The abducens (VI) nucleus with the genu (internal loop) of the facial (VII) nerve arching over it.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: What tumour classically arises at the cerebellopontine angle, and which nerves are involved?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: A vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma), involving CN VIII (hearing loss, tinnitus, imbalance) and then CN VII (and V).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: What is locked-in syndrome and where is the lesion?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: A ventral pontine (basilar artery) infarct → quadriplegia and anarthria with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: What do the pyramids of the medulla contain, and what happens at the pyramidal decussation?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: The corticospinal tracts; ~85–90% of fibres cross the midline at the pyramidal (motor) decussation in the lower medulla to form the lateral corticospinal tract.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: What are the olives, and how do CN XII and CN IX/X/XI relate to them?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: The inferior olivary nuclei (a cerebellar relay). CN XII exits anterior to the olive (between it and the pyramid); CN IX, X, XI exit posterior to the olive.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: Where do the dorsal columns synapse and decussate in the medulla?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: They synapse in the nucleus gracilis and cuneatus; their second-order fibres cross as the internal arcuate fibres to form the contralateral medial lemniscus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: Which vital centres are located in the medulla?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: The cardiovascular, respiratory and vomiting centres; the area postrema (chemoreceptor trigger zone) lacks a blood–brain barrier.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: What are the features of the lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, and its vessel?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: PICA/vertebral occlusion: ipsilateral Horner’s, facial pain/temp loss (spinal V), ataxia, dysphagia/hoarseness (IX/X); contralateral body pain/temp loss — with no limb weakness.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: What are the features of the medial medullary syndrome?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: Ipsilateral tongue weakness (CN XII) with contralateral hemiparesis and loss of proprioception/vibration (anterior spinal artery territory).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: What is the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) and what does its damage cause?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: A diffuse brainstem network that maintains consciousness and the sleep–wake cycle; its damage (or bilateral thalamic injury) causes coma.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: Which monoaminergic nuclei lie in the brainstem reticular formation?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: The raphe nuclei (serotonin) and the locus coeruleus (noradrenaline), among the reticular and autonomic nuclei.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: Which cranial-nerve nucleus mediates taste and general visceral sensation, and from which nerves?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: The nucleus of the solitary tract in the medulla — receiving taste and visceral afferents from CN VII, IX and X.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.front: Which nuclei give the branchial (special visceral) motor supply, and to what?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.back: The motor nucleus of V (muscles of mastication), the facial motor nucleus (muscles of facial expression) and the nucleus ambiguus (pharynx/larynx via IX, X, XI).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: What modalities does the dorsal column–medial lemniscus (DCML) pathway carry?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: Fine (discriminative) touch, vibration, proprioception and two-point discrimination.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: Trace the three neurons of the DCML pathway.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: 1st-order: DRG → ascends the ipsilateral dorsal column → nucleus gracilis/cuneatus (medulla). 2nd-order: decussates as the internal arcuate fibres → medial lemniscus → VPL thalamus. 3rd-order: VPL → postcentral gyrus (3,1,2).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: Which dorsal column carries the leg, and which the arm?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: The gracile fasciculus carries the lower limb / below ~T6 (medial); the cuneate fasciculus carries the upper limb / above ~T6 (lateral).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: Where does the DCML pathway decussate?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: In the medulla — the second-order fibres cross as the internal arcuate fibres to form the contralateral medial lemniscus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: What modalities does the spinothalamic (anterolateral) pathway carry?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: The lateral spinothalamic tract carries pain & temperature; the anterior spinothalamic tract carries crude touch & pressure.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: Trace the three neurons of the spinothalamic pathway.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: 1st-order: DRG → dorsal horn. 2nd-order: decussates within 1–2 segments via the anterior white commissure → ascends the contralateral anterolateral cord → VPL thalamus. 3rd-order: VPL → postcentral gyrus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: Where does the spinothalamic pathway decussate, and why does it matter?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: It crosses at the spinal cord level (within 1–2 segments of entry) — so a cord lesion causes contralateral pain/temperature loss (in contrast to the ipsilateral DCML loss).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: Summarise the crossing-point contrast between DCML and spinothalamic.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: DCML crosses in the medulla → a cord lesion gives ipsilateral loss; spinothalamic crosses in the cord → a cord lesion gives contralateral loss. This underlies Brown–Séquard syndrome.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: Which thalamic nucleus relays body sensation, and which relays the face?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: The VPL relays body sensation (DCML + spinothalamic); the VPM relays facial sensation (trigeminal).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: Trace the upper motor neuron of the corticospinal tract.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: Primary motor cortex (area 4, Betz cells) → corona radiata → posterior limb of the internal capsule → crus cerebri → pons → medullary pyramids → decussation → lateral corticospinal tract.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: What proportion of corticospinal fibres decussate, and where?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: About 85–90% cross at the pyramidal (motor) decussation in the caudal medulla to form the lateral corticospinal tract; ~10% remain uncrossed as the anterior corticospinal tract (crossing at their segmental level).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: Where does the corticospinal upper motor neuron synapse onto the lower motor neuron?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: On the anterior (ventral) horn cell of the spinal cord; the LMN then projects to skeletal muscle — a two-neuron motor chain.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: List the signs of an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: Spastic weakness, hyperreflexia, up-going plantar (Babinski), increased tone (clasp-knife), no muscle wasting (± clonus).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: List the signs of a lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: Flaccid weakness, hyporeflexia/areflexia, marked wasting, fasciculations and reduced tone.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: Why does an UMN lesion cause forehead sparing but a contralateral lower-face droop?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: Corticobulbar fibres to the upper face are bilateral (so preserved), but those to the lower face (VII) are mainly contralateral, so an UMN lesion droops the contralateral lower face only.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: Which cranial-nerve muscles receive mainly contralateral (unilateral) corticobulbar control?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: The lower face (facial nerve) and the genioglossus (hypoglossal nerve) — so UMN lesions cause contralateral lower-facial weakness and tongue deviation away from the lesion.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: Name the extrapyramidal tracts and their general role.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: The rubrospinal, reticulospinal, vestibulospinal and tectospinal tracts — they modulate muscle tone, posture and reflexes rather than voluntary movement.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: Describe the visual pathway from retina to cortex.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: Retina → optic nerve → optic chiasm (nasal fibres cross) → optic tract → lateral geniculate nucleus → optic radiation → primary visual cortex (area 17, calcarine sulcus).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: What field defect does an optic chiasm lesion cause, and a classic cause?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: A bitemporal hemianopia (the crossing nasal fibres are interrupted) — classically from a pituitary tumour or craniopharyngioma.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: What field defect follows an optic nerve lesion versus an optic tract lesion?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: Optic nerve → monocular blindness of that eye; optic tract → contralateral homonymous hemianopia.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: What field defect results from a Meyer's loop (temporal radiation) lesion?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: A contralateral superior quadrantanopia (‘pie in the sky’) — Meyer’s loop carries the inferior retinal fibres (upper visual field).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: Why does an occipital (visual cortex) stroke spare the macula?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: The occipital pole (macular area) has a dual blood supply (MCA collaterals as well as PCA), so a PCA infarct leaves central (macular) vision intact.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: Describe the pupillary light reflex circuit.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: Afferent — CN II → both pretectal nuclei → both Edinger–Westphal nuclei; efferent — CN III (parasympathetic) → ciliary ganglion → sphincter pupillae → constriction. The bilateral projection gives the consensual response.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: What does a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD/Marcus Gunn) indicate?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: An optic nerve (afferent) lesion — on swinging the torch to the affected eye, both pupils paradoxically dilate.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: Trace the auditory pathway from cochlea to cortex.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: Cochlear hair cells → cochlear nerve (VIII) → cochlear nuclei → superior olivary nuclei (bilateral) → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate nucleus → primary auditory cortex (41,42, Heschl’s gyri).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.front: Why does a unilateral central (cortical) lesion not cause deafness?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.back: Because auditory information is bilaterally represented above the cochlear nuclei; unilateral deafness therefore implies a lesion of the ear, cochlear nerve or cochlear nucleus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: What are the two arterial systems supplying the brain?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: The anterior circulation (from the internal carotid arteries → ACA & MCA) and the posterior circulation (from the vertebral → basilar arteries → PCA).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: List the main branches of the internal carotid artery.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: The ophthalmic artery, posterior communicating artery, anterior choroidal artery, and the terminal anterior (ACA) and middle (MCA) cerebral arteries.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: What do the lenticulostriate arteries supply, and which vessel gives them?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: Branches of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) supplying the internal capsule and basal ganglia — the vessels of lacunar strokes and hypertensive (Charcot–Bouchard) haemorrhage.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: What does occlusion of the ophthalmic artery (or its central retinal branch) cause?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: Monocular visual loss — transient (amaurosis fugax) or permanent (central retinal artery occlusion).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: Trace the posterior (vertebrobasilar) circulation.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: The two vertebral arteries (from the subclavians) give the PICA and spinal arteries, then unite to form the basilar artery, which gives AICA, pontine branches and the SCA before bifurcating into the two posterior cerebral arteries.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: Which cerebellar artery supplies the lateral medulla, and what syndrome does its occlusion cause?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: The posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) — occlusion causes the lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: What does the AICA supply, and what deficit can its occlusion cause?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: The lateral pons (and via the labyrinthine artery, the inner ear) → CN VII & VIII signs including ipsilateral deafness/vertigo and facial weakness.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: What does the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) supply, and what does its occlusion cause?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: The occipital lobe (and inferomedial temporal lobe) → a contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: What forms the anterior part of the circle of Willis?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: The two anterior cerebral arteries (ACAs) joined by the single anterior communicating artery (ACom).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: What forms the posterior part of the circle of Willis?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: Each posterior cerebral artery (PCA) joined to the internal carotid artery by a posterior communicating artery (PCom).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: What is the functional importance of the circle of Willis?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: It provides collateral (anastomotic) flow between the anterior and posterior circulations if one vessel is occluded — although it is often anatomically incomplete/variant.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: What is the deficit of an anterior cerebral artery (ACA) stroke?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: Contralateral weakness & sensory loss of the leg > arm (the leg lies on the medial homunculus), ± abulia.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: What is the deficit of a middle cerebral artery (MCA) stroke?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: Contralateral face/arm > leg weakness/sensory loss, with aphasia (dominant) or hemineglect (non-dominant).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: What are watershed zones and when do they infarct?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: Border regions between adjacent arterial territories (ACA/MCA and MCA/PCA); they infarct in global hypoperfusion (severe hypotension/cardiac arrest) → proximal-limb (‘man-in-a-barrel’) weakness.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: Where do berry (saccular) aneurysms form, and which is the commonest site?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: At branch points of the circle of Willis; the commonest site is the anterior communicating artery.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: What deficit classically results from a posterior communicating artery aneurysm?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: A CN III palsy — a painful, pupil-involving (‘blown pupil’) third-nerve palsy from compression.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: What are the risk factors for berry aneurysm/subarachnoid haemorrhage?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: Polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, coarctation of the aorta, smoking and hypertension.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: What are Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms and what do they cause?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: Microaneurysms on the small penetrating (lenticulostriate) arteries in chronic hypertension → deep intracerebral haemorrhage (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: Describe the venous drainage of the brain from cortex to internal jugular vein.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: Superficial veins → superior sagittal sinus; deep veins → great cerebral vein of Galen → straight sinus; both reach the confluence of sinuses → transverse → sigmoid → internal jugular vein.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: What is the role of arachnoid granulations?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: They project into the superior sagittal sinus and return CSF to the venous blood (their blockage causes communicating hydrocephalus).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: Which veins tear in a subdural haematoma?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: The bridging (cortical) veins that cross from the cortex to the superior sagittal sinus — vulnerable in the elderly/atrophic brain.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: What is cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and its risk factors?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: Thrombosis of a dural sinus → raised ICP, headache, seizures and venous infarction; risk factors include pregnancy/puerperium, dehydration, the COCP and prothrombotic states.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: What structures run in the LATERAL WALL of the cavernous sinus?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: Cranial nerves III, IV, V₁ and V₂ (from superior to inferior).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: What structures run THROUGH (inside) the cavernous sinus?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: The internal carotid artery (the most medial content) and CN VI (abducens), which runs free in the sinus lumen alongside the ICA — the reason CN VI is often the first cranial nerve affected in thrombosis.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: What is cavernous sinus thrombosis, and how does it present?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: Thrombosis (often from facial/orbital sepsis via the valveless facial veins — the ‘danger triangle’) → painful ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, chemosis and palsies of CN III, IV, VI and V₁/V₂.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.front: Why can facial infection spread to the cavernous sinus?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.back: The facial vein is valveless and connects (via the ophthalmic veins) to the cavernous sinus, allowing retrograde spread of infection from the ‘danger triangle’ of the face.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: How many ventricles are there, and what are they?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: Four: two lateral ventricles (one per hemisphere), the third ventricle (midline, between the thalami) and the fourth ventricle (between pons/medulla and cerebellum).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: What lines the ventricles, and what produces the CSF?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: The ventricles are lined by ependyma; CSF is produced by the choroid plexus (modified ependymal cells), mostly in the two lateral ventricles.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: Through what does each lateral ventricle drain into the third ventricle?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: The interventricular foramen (of Monro).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: What connects the third and fourth ventricles?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: The cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius), which runs through the midbrain — the narrowest part of the ventricular system.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: Through which foramina does CSF leave the fourth ventricle?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: The paired lateral foramina of Luschka and the single median foramen of Magendie → into the subarachnoid space.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: Trace the full path of CSF flow from production to reabsorption.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: Choroid plexus → lateral ventricles → foramen of Monro → 3rd ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → 4th ventricle → foramina of Luschka & Magendie → subarachnoid space → arachnoid granulations → dural venous sinuses.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: Where is CSF reabsorbed into the venous blood?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: At the arachnoid granulations (villi), which project into the dural venous sinuses (especially the superior sagittal sinus); reabsorption is one-way and pressure-dependent.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: What are the approximate total CSF volume, daily production and turnover?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: Total volume ≈ 150 mL; production ≈ 500 mL/day — so the whole pool is turned over ~3–4 times a day.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: List the main functions of CSF.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: Buoyancy (the ~1400 g brain effectively weighs only ~50 g), cushioning/shock absorption, homeostasis (stable ionic environment) and waste clearance (glymphatic).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: How does normal CSF composition compare with plasma?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: Clear & colourless; glucose ≈ ⅔ of plasma; low protein (~0.15–0.45 g/L); few cells (0–5 lymphocytes/µL, no neutrophils/RBCs normally).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: What is the normal CSF opening pressure on lumbar puncture in an adult?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: About 7–18 cmH₂O (lying down).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: Define non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus and give causes.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: A block within the ventricular system, so only the ventricles proximal to the block dilate. Causes: aqueduct stenosis, posterior fossa tumour, colloid cyst at the foramen of Monro.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: Define communicating hydrocephalus and give causes.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: CSF leaves the ventricles but reabsorption fails at the arachnoid granulations, so all ventricles dilate. Causes: post-meningitis or post-subarachnoid haemorrhage scarring; rarely overproduction (choroid plexus papilloma).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: Which single site is the classic location for obstructive hydrocephalus, and why?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: The cerebral aqueduct — it is the narrowest part of the ventricular system, so aqueduct stenosis readily causes non-communicating hydrocephalus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: What is normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) and its classic triad?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: A communicating hydrocephalus of the elderly with a normal opening pressure. Triad (‘wet, wobbly, wacky’): urinary incontinence + gait apraxia + dementia; potentially reversible with a VP shunt.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: What are the features of raised intracranial pressure?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: Headache (worse lying/coughing), vomiting, papilloedema, falling GCS, and eventually brain herniation (coning).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: What is Cushing's triad and what does it signify?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: Hypertension (wide pulse pressure), bradycardia and irregular breathing — a pre-terminal sign of dangerously raised intracranial pressure.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: Why must a lumbar puncture be avoided when there is a mass lesion or raised ICP?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: Releasing CSF pressure below the block can precipitate fatal tonsillar herniation (coning) — so obtain a CT head first.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: At what level is a lumbar puncture performed, and why is it safe there?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: At L3/L4 or L4/L5, below the conus medullaris (which ends at ~L1/L2 in adults), so the needle enters the cauda equina where the nerve roots float aside.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: What surface landmark marks the L4 level for a lumbar puncture?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: The intercristal (Tuffier’s) line joining the tops of the iliac crests (~L4 / the L4/5 interspace).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: What is the difference between an EVD and a VP shunt?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: An EVD (external ventricular drain) is an emergency temporary drain of CSF to the outside; a VP shunt (ventriculoperitoneal) is a long-term internal diversion of CSF to the peritoneal cavity.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.front: What is the shape and position of the fourth ventricle?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.back: A diamond-shaped cavity lying between the pons/medulla (anteriorly) and the cerebellum (posteriorly); it continues below as the central canal of the spinal cord.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.question: A right MCA stroke would most likely cause:
options: Right face and arm weakness with aphasia
Left face and arm weakness with hemineglect
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.explanation: The MCA supplies the lateral hemisphere (face/arm homunculus); a right MCA stroke causes left face/arm weakness and, being non-dominant, hemineglect.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.question: Weakness affecting the leg more than the arm suggests a stroke of the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.explanation: The ACA supplies the medial hemisphere where the leg is represented on the homunculus, so ACA strokes cause leg > arm weakness.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.question: A pure motor hemiparesis with no aphasia, neglect or visual loss suggests a:
options: Lacunar infarct of the internal capsule
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Lacunar infarcts (deep perforators, e.g. posterior limb of the internal capsule) cause pure motor or pure sensory syndromes with no cortical signs.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.question: A lesion causing an ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy with contralateral limb weakness localises to the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Crossed signs (ipsilateral cranial nerve + contralateral long-tract) are the hallmark of a brainstem lesion.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.question: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome is caused by occlusion of the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Wallenberg syndrome results from PICA/vertebral occlusion, causing ipsilateral Horner's, facial sensory loss, ataxia and dysphagia with contralateral body sensory loss.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.question: Non-fluent, effortful speech with intact comprehension is characteristic of:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Broca's aphasia (inferior frontal gyrus) produces non-fluent, effortful speech with preserved comprehension ('Broca = broken speech').

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.question: An upper motor neuron (e.g. stroke) facial palsy differs from a lower motor neuron (Bell's) palsy in that it:
options: Affects the whole half of the face
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.explanation: The upper face has bilateral cortical input, so a UMN lesion spares the forehead; an LMN (CN VII) lesion paralyses the entire half of the face.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.question: In Brown-Séquard syndrome, loss of pain and temperature sensation is:
options: Contralateral to the lesion, 1–2 levels below
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.explanation: The spinothalamic tract crosses within a couple of segments, so pain/temperature loss is contralateral; motor and dorsal-column loss are ipsilateral.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.question: Anterior spinal artery (anterior cord) syndrome spares:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.explanation: The dorsal columns are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries and are spared; the anterior two-thirds (motor + spinothalamic) is infarcted.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.question: A 'cape-like' loss of pain and temperature with arms weaker than legs suggests:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Central cord syndrome (e.g. syrinx or hyperextension) produces a suspended 'cape' sensory loss and upper > lower limb weakness.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.question: Subacute combined degeneration of the cord is caused by deficiency of:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency damages the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts, causing sensory ataxia with UMN weakness.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.question: A fixed, dilated pupil with a 'down-and-out' eye in a head-injured patient indicates:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Uncal (transtentorial) herniation stretches CN III, producing a fixed dilated pupil and down-and-out eye — a neurosurgical emergency.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.question: Cushing's triad of raised intracranial pressure comprises:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Cushing's triad — hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration — is a late sign of dangerously raised intracranial pressure.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.question: A biconvex (lens-shaped) haematoma that does not cross suture lines is typically:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.explanation: An extradural haematoma from the middle meningeal artery is biconvex and limited by sutures; a classic lucid interval precedes deterioration.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.question: A crescent-shaped haemorrhage crossing suture lines in an elderly anticoagulated patient is a:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.explanation: A subdural haematoma from torn bridging veins is crescent-shaped, crosses sutures and is common in the elderly/anticoagulated.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.question: A sudden 'thunderclap' worst-ever headache with neck stiffness suggests:
options: Subarachnoid haemorrhage from a berry aneurysm
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Subarachnoid haemorrhage, usually from a ruptured berry aneurysm of the circle of Willis, presents with a thunderclap headache and meningism.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.question: Cerebellar signs (dysdiadochokinesia, ataxia, intention tremor) are:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Cerebellar signs are ipsilateral to the lesion because the cerebellar pathways double-cross; the mnemonic DANISH captures the signs.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.question: Violent flinging movements of one side of the body (hemiballismus) result from a lesion of the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinica.explanation: Hemiballismus is caused by a lesion of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus, often a lacunar stroke.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.question: The central sulcus separates the primary motor cortex from the primary somatosensory cortex, which lie respectively in the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.explanation: The primary motor cortex is the precentral gyrus (area 4) in front of the central sulcus; the primary somatosensory cortex is the postcentral gyrus (3,1,2) behind it.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.question: The giant Betz cells of the primary motor cortex are located in cortical layer:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.explanation: Betz cells are giant pyramidal neurons in layer V, the output layer, contributing large axons to the corticospinal tract.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.question: Which cortical layer receives the main thalamic sensory input?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.explanation: Layer IV (internal granular) receives thalamic sensory afferents and is prominent in sensory 'granular' cortex, absent in motor 'agranular' cortex.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.question: The primary visual cortex corresponds to Brodmann area:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.explanation: The primary visual (striate) cortex around the calcarine sulcus is Brodmann area 17; areas 18 and 19 are visual association cortex.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.question: The primary auditory cortex (Heschl's gyri) corresponds to Brodmann areas:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.explanation: The primary auditory cortex in Heschl's gyri of the superior temporal gyrus is Brodmann areas 41 and 42, organised tonotopically.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.question: Broca's area, controlling expressive speech, is located in the:
options: Inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.explanation: Broca's area (Brodmann 44/45) is in the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere; Wernicke's (area 22) is in the posterior superior temporal gyrus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.question: Wernicke's area (language comprehension) corresponds to Brodmann area:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.explanation: Wernicke's area is Brodmann area 22 in the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.question: The tract connecting Wernicke's area to Broca's area is the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.explanation: The arcuate fasciculus (an association fibre) links Wernicke's to Broca's area; its damage causes conduction aphasia (impaired repetition).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.question: On the motor/sensory homunculus, the leg and foot are represented on the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.explanation: The leg/foot lie on the medial surface (paracentral lobule, ACA territory), so ACA strokes cause leg > arm weakness; the face/hand are lateral (MCA).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.question: Body parts are represented on the homunculus in proportion to their:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.explanation: Cortical representation is proportional to dexterity/sensitivity, so the hand, lips and face are hugely over-represented and the trunk is small.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.question: Fibres that connect cortical areas within the same hemisphere are called:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.explanation: Association fibres (e.g. arcuate, uncinate, cingulum) connect areas within one hemisphere; commissural fibres connect the two hemispheres and projection fibres link cortex to subcortex.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.question: The largest commissural tract of the brain is the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.explanation: The corpus callosum is the largest commissure, connecting the two hemispheres; its section produces 'split-brain' disconnection syndromes.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.question: The corticospinal tract descends through which part of the internal capsule?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.explanation: The corticospinal (and sensory) fibres run in the posterior limb of the internal capsule; a lacunar stroke there causes a pure motor hemiparesis.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.question: Corticobulbar fibres to the cranial-nerve motor nuclei run in the ____ of the internal capsule.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.explanation: Corticobulbar fibres run in the genu of the internal capsule; corticospinal fibres run in the posterior limb.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.question: In approximately what percentage of people is the left hemisphere dominant for language?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.explanation: The left hemisphere is dominant for language in ~95% of people, including the majority of left-handers.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.question: A lesion of the non-dominant (usually right) parietal lobe most characteristically causes:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.explanation: Non-dominant parietal lesions cause contralateral hemispatial neglect; Gerstmann's syndrome follows a dominant (angular gyrus) lesion.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.question: The frontal eye field (Brodmann area 8) controls:
options: Voluntary conjugate gaze to the opposite side
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.explanation: The frontal eye field drives voluntary conjugate gaze to the contralateral side; a destructive lesion makes the eyes deviate toward the side of the lesion.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.question: The premotor and supplementary motor areas, responsible for planning movement, are Brodmann area:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex &.explanation: Brodmann area 6 (premotor and supplementary motor cortex), just anterior to the primary motor cortex, plans and sequences movements.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.question: The striatum, the input zone of the basal ganglia, consists of the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.explanation: The striatum = caudate + putamen (the input zone); the lentiform nucleus = putamen + globus pallidus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.question: The main output nuclei of the basal ganglia, which tonically inhibit the thalamus, are the:
options: GPi and substantia nigra pars reticulata
Substantia nigra pars compacta and GPe
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.explanation: The internal globus pallidus (GPi) and substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) are the output nuclei; they tonically inhibit the thalamus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.question: Activation of the direct pathway (D1) results in:
options: Inhibition of the thalamus and less movement
Disinhibition of the thalamus and more movement
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.explanation: The direct pathway inhibits GPi/SNr, disinhibiting the thalamus, which then excites the cortex to promote movement.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.question: Dopamine released from the substantia nigra pars compacta:
options: Inhibits the direct and excites the indirect pathway
Excites the direct and inhibits the indirect pathway
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.explanation: Dopamine excites the direct pathway (D1) and inhibits the indirect pathway (D2); both effects promote movement, so its loss (Parkinson's) reduces movement.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.question: Parkinson's disease results from degeneration of the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.explanation: Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta produces the hypokinetic features of Parkinson's disease.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.question: Huntington's disease (chorea) is caused by loss of neurons in the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.explanation: Huntington's disease causes degeneration of GABAergic striatal (caudate) neurons of the indirect pathway, producing hyperkinetic chorea.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.question: Hemiballismus results from a lesion of the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.explanation: A lesion of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus (often lacunar) causes hemiballismus — violent flinging limb movements.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.question: Which sensory modality is NOT relayed through the thalamus?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.explanation: Olfaction is the only sensory modality that reaches the cortex without a thalamic relay; all others synapse in the thalamus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.question: Facial sensation and taste are relayed by which thalamic nucleus?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.explanation: The VPM (ventral posteromedial) nucleus relays facial (trigeminal) sensation and taste; the VPL relays body sensation.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.question: The lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) relays which modality, and to where?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.explanation: The LGN relays vision from the optic tract to the primary visual cortex (area 17) via the optic radiation; the MGN relays hearing.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.question: Motor information from the basal ganglia and cerebellum is relayed to the motor cortex by the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.explanation: The ventral anterior (VA) and ventral lateral (VL) nuclei relay basal ganglia and cerebellar output to the motor and premotor cortex.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.question: A stroke of the VPL/VPM causing contralateral sensory loss and later burning central pain is:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.explanation: Déjerine–Roussy (thalamic pain) syndrome follows a VPL/VPM thalamic stroke, causing contralateral sensory loss then severe central post-stroke pain.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.question: The only output neuron of the cerebellar cortex is the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.explanation: The Purkinje cell is the sole output of the cerebellar cortex and is inhibitory (GABAergic), projecting to the deep cerebellar nuclei.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.question: Which deep cerebellar nucleus is the most lateral?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.explanation: From lateral to medial the deep nuclei are Dentate, Emboliform, Globose, Fastigial ('Don't Eat Greasy Food'), so the dentate is most lateral.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.question: The flocculonodular lobe (vestibulocerebellum) is chiefly concerned with:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.explanation: The vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe) controls balance and coordination of eye movements via vestibular connections.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.question: Which cerebellar peduncle is predominantly efferent (carrying output to the red nucleus and thalamus)?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.explanation: The superior cerebellar peduncle is mainly efferent, carrying dentatorubrothalamic fibres to the red nucleus and thalamus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.question: Cerebellar signs are ipsilateral to the lesion because the output:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.explanation: Cerebellar output double-crosses (dentatorubrothalamic decussation then corticospinal decussation), so a hemisphere lesion produces ipsilateral signs.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.question: A midline (vermis) cerebellar lesion characteristically causes:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (.explanation: A vermis/midline lesion causes truncal and gait ataxia (e.g. alcohol, medulloblastoma); hemisphere lesions cause ipsilateral limb ataxia.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.question: The cranial nerves arising from the midbrain are:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.explanation: The midbrain gives rise to the oculomotor (III) and trochlear (IV) nerves; the pons gives V–VIII and the medulla IX, X, XII.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.question: Within the brainstem, motor cranial-nerve nuclei lie ____ and sensory nuclei lie ____ relative to the sulcus limitans.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.explanation: Motor nuclei (basal plate derivatives) lie medial to the sulcus limitans and sensory nuclei (alar plate) lie lateral.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.question: Which cranial nerve is the only one to exit the brainstem on its dorsal surface?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.explanation: The trochlear nerve (IV) is the only cranial nerve to emerge from the dorsal surface of the brainstem, and it decussates before exiting.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.question: The superior colliculus of the midbrain is concerned with ____, while the inferior colliculus is a relay for ____.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.explanation: The superior colliculus mediates visual reflexes/eye movements and the inferior colliculus is an auditory relay (to the medial geniculate).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.question: The corticospinal tracts descend through which midbrain structure?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.explanation: The cerebral peduncles (crura cerebri) carry the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts; the substantia nigra lies just behind them.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.question: Weber's syndrome (midbrain) produces:
options: Ipsilateral CN VI palsy + contralateral hemiparesis
Ipsilateral CN XII palsy + contralateral hemiparesis
Ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral hemiparesis
Contralateral CN III palsy + ipsilateral hemiparesis
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.explanation: Weber's syndrome from a cerebral peduncle lesion gives an ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral hemiparesis (a crossed sign).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.question: The facial colliculus on the floor of the fourth ventricle is formed by the abducens nucleus and the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.explanation: The facial colliculus is produced by the internal genu of the facial (VII) nerve looping over the abducens (VI) nucleus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.question: A tumour at the cerebellopontine angle (vestibular schwannoma) first affects which cranial nerve?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.explanation: A vestibular schwannoma arises from CN VIII, causing sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance, later involving VII and V.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.question: Locked-in syndrome results from an infarct of the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.explanation: A ventral pontine (basilar artery) infarct causes locked-in syndrome: quadriplegia and anarthria with preserved consciousness and vertical gaze.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.question: The corticospinal tracts cross the midline at the:
options: Pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.explanation: About 85–90% of corticospinal fibres decussate at the pyramidal (motor) decussation in the caudal medulla to form the lateral corticospinal tract.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.question: The hypoglossal nerve (XII) emerges from the medulla:
options: Between the pyramid and the olive
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.explanation: CN XII exits in the anterolateral sulcus between the pyramid and the olive; CN IX, X and XI exit posterior to the olive.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.question: Second-order dorsal column fibres decussate in the medulla as the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.explanation: After synapsing in the nucleus gracilis and cuneatus, dorsal-column fibres cross as the internal arcuate fibres to form the contralateral medial lemniscus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.question: The area postrema of the medulla is clinically important because it:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.explanation: The area postrema is the chemoreceptor trigger zone for vomiting and lacks a blood-brain barrier, so it senses blood-borne emetic stimuli.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.question: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome characteristically spares:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.explanation: Wallenberg syndrome (PICA/vertebral) does not affect the pyramid, so limb power is preserved; ipsilateral Horner's, facial sensory loss, ataxia and dysphagia occur.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.question: The nucleus of the solitary tract receives taste and visceral afferents from cranial nerves:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.explanation: The nucleus of the solitary tract in the medulla receives taste and general visceral sensation from the facial (VII), glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) nerves.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.question: The ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) is essential for:
options: Maintaining consciousness and the sleep-wake cycle
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.explanation: The ARAS maintains consciousness and arousal; damage to it (or to both thalami) causes coma.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.question: Which cranial nerves are found at the pons?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.explanation: The pons contains the trigeminal (V), abducens (VI), facial (VII) and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.question: Medial medullary syndrome (anterior spinal artery) causes ipsilateral weakness of the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem.explanation: Medial medullary syndrome damages the hypoglossal nucleus/nerve, causing ipsilateral tongue weakness, plus contralateral hemiparesis and proprioceptive loss.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.question: The dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway carries all of the following EXCEPT:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.explanation: Pain and temperature travel in the spinothalamic (anterolateral) pathway; the DCML carries fine touch, vibration, proprioception and two-point discrimination.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.question: The DCML pathway decussates in the:
options: Spinal cord at the level of entry
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.explanation: Second-order DCML fibres decussate in the medulla as the internal arcuate fibres to form the contralateral medial lemniscus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.question: The lateral spinothalamic tract carries:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.explanation: The lateral spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature; the anterior spinothalamic tract carries crude touch and pressure.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.question: The spinothalamic tract decussates:
options: In the spinal cord within 1–2 segments
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.explanation: Spinothalamic second-order fibres cross within 1–2 segments of entry via the anterior white commissure, then ascend contralaterally to the VPL.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.question: A left spinal cord hemisection (Brown-Séquard) causes loss of pain and temperature on the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.explanation: Because the spinothalamic tract has already crossed, hemisection causes contralateral pain/temperature loss below the lesion; dorsal-column loss is ipsilateral.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.question: Body sensation is relayed to the cortex by which thalamic nucleus?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.explanation: The VPL relays body sensation (DCML and spinothalamic) to the primary somatosensory cortex; the VPM relays facial sensation.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.question: The corticospinal tract passes through which part of the internal capsule?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.explanation: The corticospinal fibres descend through the posterior limb of the internal capsule (corticobulbar fibres run in the genu).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.question: Approximately what proportion of corticospinal fibres decussate at the pyramidal decussation?
