anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.explanation: Roughly 85–90% of corticospinal fibres cross at the pyramidal decussation to form the lateral corticospinal tract; ~10% remain as the anterior corticospinal tract.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.question: Which set of signs indicates an upper motor neuron lesion?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.explanation: UMN lesions cause spastic weakness, hyperreflexia and an up-going plantar (Babinski) with no wasting; LMN lesions cause flaccidity, hyporeflexia, wasting and fasciculations.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.question: An upper motor neuron facial (corticobulbar) lesion spares the forehead because:
options: The forehead has no motor supply
The facial nerve is not involved
The upper face receives bilateral cortical input
The lesion is in the pons
The forehead is supplied by CN V
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.explanation: The upper face receives bilateral corticobulbar input, so it is spared in a UMN lesion; the lower face (mainly contralateral input) droops.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.question: At the optic chiasm, the fibres that decussate are from the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.explanation: Nasal retinal fibres (carrying the temporal visual fields) cross at the chiasm; a central chiasmal lesion therefore causes a bitemporal hemianopia.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.question: A pituitary tumour compressing the optic chiasm classically causes:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.explanation: Compression of the crossing nasal fibres at the chiasm produces a bitemporal hemianopia.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.question: A lesion of Meyer's loop in the temporal lobe produces a contralateral:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.explanation: Meyer's loop carries inferior retinal fibres (upper visual field), so its lesion causes a contralateral superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky').

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.question: An occipital cortex (PCA) infarct causes a homonymous hemianopia with:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.explanation: The macular (occipital pole) region has dual MCA/PCA supply, so a PCA occipital infarct spares macular (central) vision.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.question: In the pupillary light reflex, the afferent and efferent limbs are carried by:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.explanation: The afferent limb is the optic nerve (CN II) and the efferent limb is the parasympathetic oculomotor nerve (CN III) via the ciliary ganglion to the sphincter pupillae.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.question: A relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil) indicates a lesion of the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.explanation: A RAPD reflects an optic (afferent) nerve lesion: swinging the light to the affected eye makes both pupils dilate because the afferent signal is weak.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.question: Which is the correct order of the auditory pathway?
options: Cochlear nerve → inferior colliculus → superior olive → MGN → cortex
Cochlear nerve → cochlear nuclei → superior olive → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → MGN → cortex
Cochlear nerve → MGN → inferior colliculus → cortex
Cochlear nerve → LGN → superior olive → cortex
Cochlear nerve → cochlear nuclei → LGN → cortex
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.explanation: The pathway runs: cochlear nerve → cochlear nuclei → superior olive → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate nucleus → auditory cortex (41/42).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.question: A unilateral lesion of the primary auditory cortex does NOT cause deafness because:
options: The cortex is not involved in hearing
Both ears share one cochlear nerve
Auditory information is bilaterally represented above the cochlear nuclei
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory.explanation: Because auditory pathways are bilateral above the cochlear nuclei, a unilateral cortical lesion does not cause deafness; unilateral deafness implies an ear/cochlear nerve/nucleus lesion.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.question: The anterior circulation of the brain is supplied by the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.explanation: The internal carotid arteries supply the anterior circulation (giving the ACA and MCA); the vertebrobasilar system supplies the posterior circulation.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.question: The lenticulostriate arteries, which supply the internal capsule and basal ganglia, arise from the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.explanation: The lenticulostriate branches of the MCA supply the internal capsule and basal ganglia and are the vessels of lacunar strokes and hypertensive haemorrhage.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.question: The two vertebral arteries unite to form the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.explanation: The vertebral arteries join at the pontomedullary junction to form the basilar artery, which later bifurcates into the posterior cerebral arteries.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.question: Occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) causes the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.explanation: PICA occlusion causes the lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome — ipsilateral Horner's, facial sensory loss, ataxia and dysphagia with contralateral body sensory loss.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.question: The posterior cerebral artery mainly supplies the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.explanation: The PCA supplies the occipital lobe (vision) and inferomedial temporal lobe; its occlusion causes a homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.question: The anterior communicating artery connects the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.explanation: The single anterior communicating artery joins the two anterior cerebral arteries, completing the anterior part of the circle of Willis.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.question: The posterior communicating artery connects the ____ to the ____.
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.explanation: Each posterior communicating artery links the internal carotid artery to the posterior cerebral artery, joining the anterior and posterior circulations.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.question: The single most common site of a berry (saccular) aneurysm is the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.explanation: The anterior communicating artery is the commonest site of a berry aneurysm; rupture causes subarachnoid haemorrhage.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.question: A painful third-nerve palsy with a dilated pupil suggests an aneurysm of the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.explanation: A posterior communicating artery aneurysm compresses the adjacent CN III, causing a painful, pupil-involving third-nerve palsy.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.question: Watershed (border-zone) infarcts typically result from:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.explanation: Watershed zones between arterial territories infarct during global hypoperfusion (e.g. cardiac arrest/severe hypotension), classically causing proximal-limb 'man-in-a-barrel' weakness.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.question: Deep cerebral veins drain into the straight sinus via the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.explanation: The deep cerebral veins converge on the great cerebral vein of Galen, which drains into the straight sinus; superficial veins drain to the superior sagittal sinus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.question: The dural venous sinuses ultimately drain into the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.explanation: The sinuses drain via the confluence → transverse → sigmoid sinuses into the internal jugular vein.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.question: Arachnoid granulations return which fluid to the venous blood?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.explanation: Arachnoid granulations project into the superior sagittal sinus and return CSF to the venous blood; their obstruction causes communicating hydrocephalus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.question: Which cranial nerves run in the LATERAL WALL of the cavernous sinus?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.explanation: CN III, IV, V1 and V2 run in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus; CN VI and the internal carotid artery run through the sinus itself.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.question: Which cranial nerve runs free within the cavernous sinus alongside the internal carotid artery and is often affected first in thrombosis?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.explanation: CN VI runs free within the sinus lumen adjacent to the internal carotid artery (the other nerves are embedded in the protective lateral wall), so it is typically the first cranial nerve affected in cavernous sinus thrombosis.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.question: Cavernous sinus thrombosis often arises from facial infection because the facial vein is:
options: Valveless and connects to the cavernous sinus
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.explanation: The valveless facial vein communicates (via the ophthalmic veins) with the cavernous sinus, allowing retrograde spread of infection from the facial 'danger triangle'.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.question: Bridging veins that tear to cause a subdural haematoma drain the cortex into the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.explanation: Cortical bridging veins cross the subdural space to reach the superior sagittal sinus; their rupture (e.g. in the elderly) causes a subdural haematoma.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.question: Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms, a cause of deep intracerebral haemorrhage, are associated with:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply.explanation: Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms form on small lenticulostriate perforators in chronic hypertension and rupture to cause deep (basal ganglia) intracerebral haemorrhage.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.question: Cerebrospinal fluid is produced mainly by the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.explanation: The choroid plexus (modified ependymal cells), mostly in the lateral ventricles, produces CSF; the arachnoid granulations reabsorb it.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.question: The lateral ventricles drain into the third ventricle through the:
options: Foramen of Monro into the fourth ventricle
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.explanation: Each lateral ventricle drains into the third ventricle via the interventricular foramen of Monro.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.question: The third and fourth ventricles are connected by the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius, in the midbrain, connects the third and fourth ventricles and is the narrowest part of the system.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.question: CSF leaves the fourth ventricle to reach the subarachnoid space through the foramina of:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.explanation: The two lateral foramina of Luschka and the median foramen of Magendie allow CSF to pass from the fourth ventricle into the subarachnoid space.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.question: CSF is reabsorbed into the venous blood at the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.explanation: The arachnoid granulations project into the dural venous sinuses (mainly the superior sagittal sinus) and reabsorb CSF in a one-way, pressure-dependent manner.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.question: The approximate total volume of CSF in an adult is:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.explanation: Total CSF volume is ~150 mL, but ~500 mL is produced per day, so the pool is turned over about 3–4 times daily.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.question: Compared with plasma, normal CSF glucose is:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.explanation: Normal CSF glucose is about two-thirds of the plasma level; a markedly low CSF glucose suggests bacterial (or TB/fungal) meningitis.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.question: The narrowest part of the ventricular system, and the classic site of obstructive hydrocephalus, is the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct is the narrowest channel; aqueduct stenosis is a classic cause of non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.question: In communicating hydrocephalus:
options: There is a block at the aqueduct
The ventricles are normal in size
All ventricles dilate because reabsorption fails
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.explanation: In communicating hydrocephalus CSF leaves the ventricles but reabsorption fails at the arachnoid granulations (e.g. after meningitis/SAH), so all ventricles dilate.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.question: A colloid cyst obstructing a foramen of Monro would cause:
options: Dilatation of the fourth ventricle only
Dilatation of the lateral ventricle(s) proximal to the block
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.explanation: A block at the foramen of Monro causes dilatation of the lateral ventricle(s) proximal to it — a non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.question: The classic triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus is:
options: Urinary incontinence, gait apraxia and dementia
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.explanation: NPH ('wet, wobbly, wacky') presents with urinary incontinence, a magnetic/shuffling gait apraxia and dementia, with a normal opening pressure; it may be reversible with a VP shunt.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.question: Cushing's triad, a sign of dangerously raised intracranial pressure, comprises:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.explanation: Cushing's triad — hypertension (wide pulse pressure), bradycardia and irregular breathing — is a pre-terminal sign of raised ICP.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.question: A lumbar puncture should be avoided in a patient with a mass lesion and raised ICP because it may cause:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.explanation: Releasing CSF pressure below an intracranial block can precipitate fatal tonsillar herniation (coning); a CT head should be done first.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.question: A lumbar puncture is performed at the L3/4 or L4/5 interspace because:
options: The vertebral canal is widest there
There is no CSF above L3
The cauda equina is absent below L3
It is below the conus medullaris (which ends at ~L1/L2)
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.explanation: The spinal cord (conus medullaris) ends at ~L1/L2 in adults, so a needle at L3/4 or L4/5 enters the CSF-filled cauda equina without damaging the cord.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.question: The intercristal (Tuffier's) line joining the iliac crests marks approximately the level of:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.explanation: Tuffier's line between the tops of the iliac crests marks approximately the L4 vertebra / L4-5 interspace, guiding lumbar puncture.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.question: The fourth ventricle lies between the:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.explanation: The diamond-shaped fourth ventricle lies between the pons and medulla (anteriorly) and the cerebellum (posteriorly).

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.question: Which of the following normally reduces the effective weight of the brain from ~1400 g to about 50 g?
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.explanation: CSF provides buoyancy, so the brain effectively 'weighs' only ~50 g when suspended, protecting it from its own weight.

anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.question: A choroid plexus papilloma can cause hydrocephalus by:
anatomy__NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF.explanation: A choroid plexus papilloma is a rare cause of communicating hydrocephalus through CSF overproduction (it can also obstruct if it grows large).
